title: Wish Someone Told Me This When I First Started Working on SAP Part 1
author: JENITA_04
text:
If you're new to SAP, or you've landed on a project and don't recognize half the vocabulary, this series is for you. 
 When I started, I assumed the hard part would be learning my module. It wasn't. It was the terminology: SAP, ECC, S/4HANA, Cloud, Greenfield, Brownfield, System Conversion, Upgrade, Quality, Production. I could look up each term, but I couldn't see how they fit together. It felt like collecting puzzle pieces without the picture on the box. 
 So I went back to basics and asked a few simple questions. What is SAP? Why do companies need it? Where does S/4HANA fit? Where is a customer starting from, and how do they get where they want to go? Who is involved, and where does the work actually happen? 
 This series is the mental map I built from those answers. Part 1 covers the foundation: what SAP is, what S/4HANA is, and how a customer's starting point shapes the way it transforms. Terms like Update, Upgrade, and the system landscape (Quality, Production) come in Part 2. No prior SAP knowledge is needed.

title: Real-World Learnings from Early adopters of Brownfield HPA (I_SAPIBP2) Migration
author: Kavyanshi
text:
With the introduction of the migration tool (MOVE2H) in 2605, customers already running on SAP7 or SAP7F planning areas could migrate to the new planning area : I_SAPIBP2. Two such customers adopted this brownfield migration as part of SAP’s Early Adopter Care (EAC) program. 
 Both customers have now gone live on I_SAPIBP2. This blog draws directly from their shared experiences to give you a practical, honest guide to what a brownfield HPA migration involves — what to prepare for, what to watch out for, and what the payoff looks like on the other side. 
 Customer Story 1: A Large Battery Distribution Company 
 The Business Challenge 
 The company had been running IBP successfully for years — demand planning, supply and response planning (RNS), inventory optimization (IO), and order-based planning (OBP) were all live. But one critical capability was missing: meaningful scenario planning. 
 Planners were forced to work across seven spreadsheets simultaneously to simulate different supply and demand outcomes. The process was slow, error-prone, and provided no consolidated visibility. 
 The Core Technical Challenge: Dual Product Hierarchies 
 The most significant technical complexity in this migration was a fundamental design reality: the company operates with different product numbering on the demand and supply sides. 
 Demand side: Demand Planning runs on sales part numbers, planned at the location, customer, and distributor level. 
 Supply side: Supply Planning, IO, and OBP run on vendor part numbers 
 Because the standard HPA migration tool assumes consistent product hierarchies across planning areas, it could not be used for a full automated migration. The tool was leveraged only for the Response & Supply planning area; demand planning and IO required full manual configuration from scratch within the new Harmonized Planning Area. 
 The team solved this by constructing the unified HPA in five steps: 
 Demand Planning in I_SAPIBP2 — A parallel set of sales-part product master data tables was created to support demand forecasting within the HPA. 
 Supply Planning in I_SAPIBP2 — Standard product master data tables were used for vendor-part supply, IO, and OBP planning. 
 Forecast Translation — The forecast generated on the sales part is transferred to the vendor part via a structured mapping process using CI-DS task lists. 
 Scenario Planning Architecture — Additional key figures allow planners to adjust the forecast, with scenario planning connected end-to-end through to supply planning on the vendor part. 
 Customer Data Integration — OBP customers are integrated through Real-Time Integration (RTI); the demand-to-supply handoff operates at the product-location level, keeping the design clean. 
 Scenario Planning: Before vs. After 
 Before migrating to I_SAPIBP2, bridging three separate planning areas required CI-DS jobs and copy operators to pass data across boundaries. This was functional but fragile and gave planners no consolidated view. 
 After the migration, scenario planning runs through application jobs in two modes: 
 Self-service: On-demand by planners: A dedicated application job template lets planners execute scenario runs themselves, end-to-end, at any time. 
 Scheduled: Automated background jobs handle mass data updates nightly, without overwriting any interactive key figure adjustments planners have made 
 Critical Prerequisite: HANA to HANA Cloud Upgrade 
 A prerequisite that was not initially on the project radar: The underlying database requires upgrade from SAP HANA to SAP HANA Cloud which is a mandatory pre-requisite for HPA and subsequently scenario planning. This upgrade must be completed before the migrating tool can be activated and before SAP can grant the necessary authorizations. 
 Customer Story 2: Global HVAC manufacturer 
 The Business Challenge 
 The customer was an early adopter of SAP 7 planning area using SDI (SAP HANA Smart Data Integration) during a previous early adoption program. Their IBP landscape comprised two major planning areas: Demand Planning on time-series and Order-Based Planning (OBP) on SAP7. The project described here is their brownfield migration from SAP7 to the new Harmonized Planning Area I_SAPIBP2 
 The company’s strategic sequencing was deliberate: migrate and stabilize supply planning first, then implement Inventory Optimization once HPA was proven in production. 
 Real-Time Integration (RTI): Critical Learnings 
 RTI integration between S4HANA and I_SAPIBP2 was one of the most valuable areas the customer shared. 
 Use CIAS — Do Not Attempt Manual RTI Setup: Customer initially tried to set up RTI manually and hit multiple roadblocks. Switching to the CIAS (Cloud Integration Automation Service) setup provided by SAP resolved every blocker and significantly fast-tracked the process. 
 Migration Tool (Move to I_SAPIBP2): What Worked and What Required Manual Effort 
 What worked well out of the box: 
 Attributes mapping — most attributes mapped automatically 
 Standard master data — mapped cleanly with no issues 
 Copy operators — migrated successfully once the planning area was activated 
 Core planning area configurations — the large majority migrated effectively 
 Time savings — after the tool became available, bulk migration activities were completed within 1–2 weeks (vs. weeks of manual work) 
 Iterative use — the tool can be re-run on the same source/target pair, enabling fix-and-remigrate without starting over 
 Challenges that required manual intervention: 

 # 
 CHALLENGE 
 FIX 

 1. 
 Time Profile Mismatch (Critical Prerequisite): Existing planning area lacked 'tech week' in the time profile; the I_SAPIBP2 target had it. 
 Download the existing planning area as a binary file. Manually update the time profile to match the target. Rebuild the planning area configuration. Then re-run the migration tool. 

 2. 
 Virtual and Reference Master Data: Virtual and reference master data in the SAP7 planning area did not migrate automatically in all cases. 
 Perform manual mapping and configuration adjustments for virtual and reference master data types. 

 3. 
 Planning Level Migration: In SAP7, planning levels do not require a source mapping for mandatory attributes. In I_SAPIBP2, this source assignment is mandatory — a structural difference that drove 1,300+ errors. 
 Create a virtual master data type for example PDS planning levels. Maintain all custom PDS attributes in virtual master data. Assign the virtual master data as the source in each affected planning level. Activate the planning levels — errors resolve once source assignments are correctly set up. 

 4. 
 Forecast Key Figures: Multiple forecast key figures (e.g., forecast unconstrained, helper key figures) were not mapped automatically by the tool. 
 Migrate all key figures that the tool can map and activate the planning area. Use the 'Compare Planning Area' function to identify any missing key figures. Manually create the missing key figures in the target planning area. 
 Note: You can add missing key figures post-migration without impact. Treat the migration as an iterative, not a one-shot, process.

 SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity provides a secure network that connects organizations with their banking partners, helping simplify bank communication and payment processing. You will explore the onboarding process for SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity and understand how organizations can establish efficient bank communications to optimize finance operations. Additionally, you will discover how SAP S/4HANA Cloud for Advanced Payment Management centralizes group payments, improves cash and treasury management, and helps organizations streamline financial operations while reducing operational costs. 
 The e-learning course consists of the following three modules, followed by a knowledge assessment:

author: djwafelap
text:

 Due to their organisational structure, my client requires a profit center in every document line in S/4HANA Public Cloud, particularly for balance sheet accounts. We were surprised to find out that in some applications it is not possible to enter a profit center, even though the profit centre is a central and crucial field in the document split.

 However, if you then try to post a bank statement or a free-form payment, neither is the profit center of the account used carried over into the posted documents, nor is there an option to enter a profit center. Instead, the system uses a dummy profit center defined in Customizing/CBC.  Kind regards, 
 Rado

title: EC to ECP Replication Error: “Employee Is Already Hired” After Rehire History Was Deleted
author: Neha_Gaur95
text:
Issue 
 An employee was originally hired and subsequently withdrawn in Employee Central (EC). This employment history was successfully replicated to Employee Central Payroll (ECP). 
 Later, the employee was rehired in EC. However, before the rehire was replicated, the original hire and withdrawal history was deleted from EC. As a result, EC contained only the latest rehire record, while ECP still contained the original employment history. 
 The replication then failed with the following errors: 
 Employee is already hired 
 Personnel number was already accounted. Do not change entry date 
 The issue occurred because the effective-dated employment history in EC was no longer aligned with the existing employee history in ECP. 
 Solution 
 Step 1: Check the EC and ECP employment history 
 Compare the employee’s effective-dated records in EC with the personnel-action history available in ECP. 
 Verify the following information: 
 Original hire date 
 Withdrawal or termination date 
 Rehire date 
 Employee status 
 Employee class and employee type 
 Existing payroll results 
 Do not change the original hire date in ECP if payroll results already exist. 
 Step 2: Restore the original employment history in EC 
 Recreate the historical records that were previously replicated to ECP: 
 Recreate the original hire record. 
 Recreate the corresponding withdrawal or termination record. 
 Verify that the events, event reasons, dates, and employment status match the records already available in ECP. 
 Complete the historical correction before recreating the latest rehire record. 
 Step 3: Correct employee classification values 
 Review the Employee Class and Employee Type values in EC. 
 Ensure that the values maintained on the hire and termination records are valid and correctly mapped to the required employee group and employee subgroup in ECP. 
 Use the appropriate values according to the organization’s EC-to-ECP mapping configuration. 
 Step 4: Verify the employee key mapping 
 In ECP, check table HRSFEC_D_EEKEYMP using transaction SE16 or SE16N . 
 Confirm that: 
 The EC employee ID is mapped to the correct ECP personnel number. 
 The employment ID and assignment details are correct. 
 No incorrect or duplicate mapping exists. 
 If the mapping is missing or inconsistent, it should be corrected through the approved SAP process. Direct table updates should not be performed without SAP guidance. 
 Step 5: Validate the earliest personnel action date 
 Check the earliest personnel action date in ECP. 
 The date should correspond to the employee’s original hire action, not the later withdrawal, termination, or rehire action. 
 If payroll results already exist, carefully assess the impact before changing the date. 
 Step 6: Run replication for the restored history 
 Trigger employee replication from EC to ECP after restoring and validating the original history. 
 Review the replication log in transaction SLG1 and confirm that: 
 The historical hire record is processed. 
 The withdrawal or termination record is processed. 
 No duplicate-hire error is generated. 
 The replicated infotype records are valid. 
 Step 7: Recreate the rehire record 
 After the original history is synchronized successfully: 
 Recreate the rehire record in EC. 
 Verify the rehire event and event reason. 
 Validate the employee classification and organizational information. 
 Trigger replication again. 
 Step 8: Validate the final result in ECP 
 After successful replication: 
 Check the personnel-action history in PA20 . 
 Confirm that the original hire, withdrawal or termination, and rehire actions appear in the correct sequence. 
 Review SLG1 to ensure that replication completed successfully. 
 Verify that the employee’s current status is correct. 
 Step 9: Validate payroll impact 
 Run payroll simulation before executing the productive payroll run. 
 If the restored historical dates generate an unexpectedly large number of retroactive payroll periods, review Infotype 0003 – Payroll Status . 
 Update the retrospective accounting date only when it is supported by the business requirement and payroll policy. Then rerun payroll and confirm that the required retroactive periods are processed correctly. 
 Conclusion 
 The error was resolved by restoring the deleted historical employment records in EC, aligning the EC and ECP histories, validating the employee-key mapping and earliest personnel action date, and then replicating the rehire record again. 
 #ECP

title: Assisted Course Generation in Learning Administration – Limitations Preventing Adoption
author: IrynaD
text:
We have been evaluating Assisted Course Generation in Learning Administration and see good potential for using AI to simplify course creation. However, we identified two current limitations that prevent us from adopting the functionality in our standard process: 
 1. Item ID generation 
 The Item ID is automatically generated, and it is currently not possible to apply the naming convention configured under System Administration → Configuration → Auto Generated IDs → Enable Item. 
 2. Mandatory Item custom fields 
 Mandatory Item custom fields using predefined drop-down values cannot be populated during the assisted course generation process. 
 These are important requirements in our LMS configuration because they support consistent course governance and data quality. As a result, courses generated through the AI-assisted functionality still require additional manual handling and do not fully align with our standard course creation process. 
 It would be helpful to know whether SAP plans to enhance Assisted Course Generation to: 
 respect the configured Item ID naming convention; and 
 support mandatory custom fields, including drop-down fields. 
 We would be interested to hear whether other SAP SuccessFactors Learning customers have encountered similar limitations and how they are managing them. 
 Thank you for feedback and comments! 
 Kind regards, 
 Iryna

title: SAP and VFC Open Intelligent Fashion Store
author: SAP News
text:
Industry AI connects the shopper journey with end-to-end retail operations, enhancing the consumer experience 

 WALLDORF — SAP SE (NYSE: SAP) and VF Corporation (NYSE: VFC) today opened S.Fashion, a retail innovation space at the SAP headquarters in Walldorf designed to explore how AI-enabled, end-to-end processes can enhance the consumer experience while making store operations more effective. 
 Autonomous Enterprise: Where your business can think, adapt and act like never before 

 Learn more 

 This store puts the SAP vision for the Autonomous Enterprise into a working fashion retail environment, with selected products from the world-renowned VF Corporation brand portfolio, including The North Face, Vans and Timberland. In this environment, Industry AI draws on business data and retail process expertise to support decisions and actions across inventory, order management, pricing, fulfillment and replenishment. The store combines these capabilities with SAP applications, automation and connected hardware. 

 The announcement was made at the opening of S.Fashion in Walldorf, attended by Christian Klein, CEO of SAP, and Sujay Kumar, Vice President, Global ERP Technology at VF Corporation. 

 “The Autonomous Enterprise becomes real when AI can understand business context and act across connected processes,” said Christian Klein, CEO of SAP. “Together with VF Corporation, we are bringing this vision to life in one of retail’s most dynamic environments. S.Fashion shows how applications, data and Industry AI can work together across the entire operation, turning insights into action while keeping people in control. When technology absorbs complexity, store teams have more time to engage with consumers and create the experiences that build lasting relationships.” 

 Industry AI Across Retail Operations 

 Fashion retail requires precise coordination across brand, style, size, color, availability, price and fulfillment. In S.Fashion, item-level RFID data, robotics and SAP applications support a connected flow across inventory, orders, pricing, promotions and replenishment. AI agents are designed to help interpret events and coordinate next steps across processes, while people retain oversight of operating rules and exceptions. By simplifying and connecting these processes, the store will explore how technology can reduce operational complexity for teams and give them greater capacity to focus on consumers. 

 A customer can discover products, explore personalization and virtual try-on options, and create an order. The process can then initiate item retrieval, customization, packing, payment and collection. The transaction updates inventory and can trigger a next step, such as replenishment, without relying on manual handoffs between separate systems. 

 The experience links the physical store with a digital journey in a mobile app. Joule, part of SAP Business AI Platform, guides consumers from store entry and product discovery to in-store navigation and checkout. At the personalization station, consumers can turn a sketch and prompt into AI-generated artwork ready for embroidery. Once ordered, the personalized garment is embroidered, packed and placed in a personal locker for pickup. A holographic virtual try-on lets consumers check fit, color and overall look without changing clothes. In the fitting room, item recognition and a smart mirror recommend sizes, matching products and styling ideas. Consumers can also request another size without leaving the room. If consumers opt in, their preferences and past interactions shape curated looks and increasingly relevant recommendations. 

 For SAP and VFC, the store serves as a live test environment for how AI, intelligent automation and physical retail work together. During selected hours, the store operates autonomously, with no staff on site. 

 “S.Fashion gives us a unique opportunity to turn retail innovation into real-world learning,” said Sujay Kumar, Vice President, Global ERP Technology at VF Corporation. “By testing new experiences in a live environment, we can better understand what resonates with consumers and what helps our teams deliver an even better experience every day. For us, technology is most valuable when it enables our people to spend more time engaging with consumers and creating meaningful in-store experiences. The insights we gain will help us learn faster, focus on what works, and scale the solutions that can make the biggest difference across our brands.” 

 An Intelligent Store Built Around Experience 

 S.Fashion is designed to explore how intelligent technology can support different retail experiences while using the same connected data and business processes across the store. The focus is on understanding how technology can complement the role of store teams, make operations more effective and create more engaging and interactive experiences for consumers. 

 During selected hours, the store operates autonomously, with no staff on site, enabling SAP and VFC to explore different retail models using the same underlying technology and processes. S.Fashion will be open to SAP employees and their friends and families, and it will also host arranged visits for customers and partners. This gives VFC and SAP a working retail environment in which to test operating processes under live conditions and demonstrate how they work together. 

 A Living Proof Point for the Autonomous Enterprise 

 The Walldorf opening puts the SAP strategy for the Autonomous Enterprise into practice in a live retail environment. This will help SAP and VFC assess how processes can recognize change, coordinate action across functions and support new commercial models.

title: ABAP Platform Becoming an Enterprise-Grade Execution Backbone for Agentic AI
author: Johannes Klostermeier
text:
In an interview, Sonja Liénard, head of ABAP Platform at SAP, discusses the Autonomous Enterprise and ABAP platform as an “execution backbone” for agentic AI. 

 About Sonja Liénard 

 Sonja Liénard is an information scientist and business information specialist who joined SAP in 2012. As senior vice president and head of ABAP Platform at SAP, she is responsible for ABAP and all matters related to ABAP platform. In this role, she is also the head of ABAP AI and thus globally responsible for the latest developments and innovations in this domain. 

 What is the Autonomous Enterprise? What part does ABAP platform play in it? 

 Liénard: At SAP Sapphire in 2026, we unveiled the Autonomous Enterprise —our vision for how we want to help large enterprises in the era of agentic AI. The fundamental shift we’re seeing is in the way people work with technology. Interfaces are no longer the focus: interaction is outcome-driven, not tool-driven. 

 The user experience is being transformed. Instead of filling out forms in an application, you simply open a chat and ask: “Who was on vacation in the last 30 days, and when?” The answer comes back in real time. That’s the Autonomous Enterprise. 

 The nature and purpose of ABAP platform is not changing. It is still the foundation on which business processes run—and it is now also the backbone on which agents operate. What is changing is the way users access applications. Agents now sit in front of those applications as an additional abstraction layer. 

 If agents are expected to handle real business tasks—not demo scenarios, but actual financial postings, HR processes, or supply chain decisions—they need to run on a platform that is reliable, governed, and scalable. 
 Get started with modern ABAP development 

 Find out how 

 Can you explain what ”outcome-driven” means? 

 Here’s an example. Instead of filling out a requisition form field by field, I open my chat and say, “I need 30 laptops for new hires by the end of October.” Agents check the catalog, review the budget, and create the requisition, without me having to navigate the process myself. 

 As a user, I’m focused solely on the outcome, not on the route I need to take. When I enter a natural-language prompt, agents can autonomously pursue a variety of solution paths. What we’re seeing is a paradigm shift. The form-based environment we’re used to is giving way to the outcome-driven, agentic model. 

 What does designing a platform for agents involve? 

 It presents us with challenges on various levels. 

 The first is reliability. Data and results must always be reliable, traceable, and reproducible—regardless of who triggered the agent or which path it took to obtain the data. This requires safety nets and very robust quality controls and tools. 

 The next level is accountability and governance. Each agent must have a clearly defined authorization scope. What is it permitted to do? What is it not permitted to do? What data is it allowed to access? Agents need skills and workflows to follow. And there must also be an audit trail: what changes an agent made, who triggered the agent, and what exactly it was instructed to do. Well-defined interfaces are essential to ensure that agents operate strictly within their architectural boundaries, helping to prevent unauthorized data flows, close potential security gaps, and protect systems from compromise. 

 And finally, there’s scalability. ABAP platform must have the computing and storage capacity required to handle spikes in agent activity. We are preparing for this, running security tests and assessing the platform’s scalability limits. 

 The key principle remains the same: we must define very clearly where and when humans retain the final say. That is the foundation of enterprise trust—in the agentic AI era as much as in any other. 

 Previously, you described the ABAP MCP (Model Context Protocol) server as an important building block for everything related to agentic AI . What’s the latest news here? 

 We released the ABAP MCP server in the second quarter. It opens ABAP platform to the agentic era by enabling MCP-compatible agents to interact with ABAP capabilities. MCP can provide well-defined interfaces for agent-to-agent communication, interaction with external tools, and task delegation. 

 You’re referring to agents that perform tasks in ABAP systems. But what about agents that administer or operate these systems? 

 We released our first AI-powered development tools in early 2025. They were designed to boost developer productivity by providing assistance with coding and with code quality reviews. We’ve now gone further. The market is moving fast, and the next logical step is to extend AI capabilities to operations. 

 We’re now looking at agents for administration and operations—and investing there, too. But we need safety nets, clear accountability, and well-defined boundaries. We will work to ensure that these agents have a supporting capacity only and that they do not operate in systems autonomously. 

 With agents handling more and more operational tasks, how will SAP ensure that the guardrails remain sufficiently robust? 

 In regards to development, it’s important to understand that ABAP and non-ABAP development differ. In ABAP, changes take effect immediately in the system and are generally corrected forward, not rolled back. This makes it especially important to have robust guardrails in place for agents, such as an isolated testing environment, thorough quality checks, and clearly defined skills and playbooks that govern agent actions and ensure reproducible results. We’re investing in all of this. 

 What about customers that are not yet on the latest release? 

 ABAP AI capabilities are now available in earlier versions as well. For enterprises looking to move to a newer release, our agent-led toolchain can offer dedicated support. We are currently building seven agent families that cover different process steps of a migration, including system analysis, testing, and custom code migration. These agents can also be deployed independently for custom code quality reviews. 

 With an eye to the rest of 2026, what should customers and partners look out for? 

 SAP is focusing on three elements. The first is migration. By year-end, we plan to ship additional practical tools to help support the entire migration process. Second is sovereign cloud solutions, for which we are developing compelling AI capabilities for enterprises with specific data sovereignty requirements. And third is MCP tooling, well-defined, secure external interfaces that open ABAP platform to the agentic world without compromising platform security. 

 You’ve been clear throughout that ABAP developers will stay relevant and that AI will not replace them. But the picture you’re painting is of a platform that increasingly runs itself. How should developers be thinking about their role? 

 How is the developer role changing? That’s a question for all developers, not just those who work on ABAP platform. Humans will continue to be responsible for what enters the system and what happens to data. We need to define clearly where humans make the final call and who is accountable. So, the role of developers is shifting. They are spending less time on writing code and more on oversight, software architecture, and prompting to ensure that agents do exactly what they are supposed to. The tasks are changing; the accountability isn’t. 

 And there’s one more point I’d like to stress: ABAP platform is becoming an enterprise-grade execution backbone for agentic AI. I use the word “backbone” deliberately. We’re not a generic agent runtime. General-purpose AI can’t match what we offer: rich, proven business logic, enterprise-grade governance, and a 40-year track record of running the world’s most critical business processes. That’s the role of ABAP platform in the Autonomous Enterprise.

title: Migrate to the Usage Records OData API (v2) — Richer Queries, Simpler Integration
author: KatherineW
text:
We'd like to share an important change to the Usage Records API: As of October 27, 2026 , the new OData API (v2) is available. The existing RESTful API (v1) was officially deprecated on November 9, 2026 and will be decommissioned on November 9, 2027 . 
 This blog explains the advantages of v2 and provides detailed instructions on migrating from v1 to v2. 
 Why the change? The v1 API used a proprietary query syntax that limited what you could do with your usage data. The v2 API is built on OData V4 , an open standard published by OASIS and adopted across the SAP product portfolio. By aligning with OData V4, the Usage Records API becomes a first-class citizen in the SAP ecosystem: 
 SAP tooling works out of the box — SAP BTP SDKs, CAP, SAP Fiori elements, and SAP Analytics Cloud all speak OData natively; no custom integration layer needed 
 Code generation — OData-aware generators can produce typed client code directly from the /$metadata endpoint 
 Broad ecosystem support — any OData V4-compatible client library, IDE extension, or BI tool (Power BI, Excel Power Query, and many open-source libraries) connects without custom adapters 
 Consistency across SAP — customers already familiar with OData from SAP S/4HANA, SAP SuccessFactors, or SAP Ariba can apply the same patterns and tooling here immediately 

 What's New in v2 
 Richer, More Flexible Data Retrieval 
 The retrieve operation is the most significant upgrade in v2. The v2 OData API introduces standard query options that give you precise control over what data is returned, and how much of it. 
 $select — Return Only the Fields You Need 
 v1 always returns all fields. With $select , you choose exactly which fields come back, reducing payload size and improving performance. GET /UsageRecords
 ?$select=ID,metricId,technicalResourceId,startedAt,endedAt,quantity,assigned 
 $expand — Navigate Related Data in a Single Request 
 v1 returns items embedded by default with no control over depth. v2 gives you full control: # Records with items and their fields
GET /UsageRecords?$expand=items($expand=fields)

# Combine $expand with $select at every level
GET /UsageRecords
 ?$select=ID,metricId,quantity
 &$expand=items(
 $select=itemNumber;
 $expand=fields($select=fieldCode,stringValue)
 ) 
 Lambda Operators — Filter by Related Entity Values 
 This was not possible in v1. OData lambda operator any lets you filter records based on the content of their related collection navigation properties. # Records with a specific custom reference type
GET /UsageRecords
 ?$filter=customReferences/any(c:c/typeCode eq 'SYSTEM_TYPE') 
 Standard $filter with New Functions 
 The proprietary filter= parameter is replaced by standard OData $filter= . All operators from v1 are supported, plus string functions: $filter=contains(metricId,'CALL')
$filter=startswith(technicalResourceId,'device-')
$filter=metricId in ('EMAIL_SENT','EMAIL_RECEIVED') 
 The total count moves from the x-count response header into the response body: GET /UsageRecords?$filter=category eq 'MEASURED'&$count=true&$top=20{
 "@context": "$metadata#UsageRecords",
 "@count": 1432,
 "value": [ ... ]
} 
 Batch Operations 
 v1 $batch used a proprietary JSON format and only supported create/upsert. v2 batch follows the standard OData V4 multipart/mixed format, supporting upsert, discard, delete, and retrieve operations in a single request. 

 Migration Guide 
 1. Update the Base URL 
 Change /v1 to /v2 in the base URL. OAuth scopes are unchanged. 

 2. Rename Changed Fields 
 v1 Field v2 Field 
 userTechnicalId technicalResourceId 
 isAssigned assigned 
 changedAt modifiedAt 
 changedBy modifiedBy 
 subscriptionNumber subscriptionDocumentNumber 
 All other field names are unchanged. 

 3. Migrate Write Operations 
 Single Record Create / Upsert 
 v1 POST /usage-records
Content-Type: application/json

{
 "category": "MEASURED",
 "metricId": "API_CALL",
 "userTechnicalId": "ce6ad4d2-...",
 "startedAt": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z",
 "endedAt": "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z",
 "quantity": 1200
} v2 POST /UsageRecords/upsertByLogicalKey
Content-Type: application/json

{
 "value": {
 "category": "MEASURED",
 "metricId": "API_CALL",
 "technicalResourceId": "ce6ad4d2-...",
 "startedAt": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z",
 "endedAt": "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z",
 "quantity": 1200
 }
} 
 Batch Operations v2 $batch — Batch upsert example 
 Note : A changeset groups write operations atomically — either all succeed or all are rolled back. It is optional; write requests can also be sent individually in a batch without a changeset. POST /$batch
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=batch_id-1778814615130-767

--batch_id-1778814615130-767
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=changeset_1

--changeset_1
Content-Type: application/http
Content-Transfer-Encoding: binary
Content-ID: 1-1

POST UsageRecords/upsertByLogicalKey HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
 "value": {
 "category": "MEASURED",
 "metricId": "API_CALL",
 "technicalResourceId": "...",
 "startedAt": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z",
 "endedAt": "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z",
 "quantity": 400
 }
}

--changeset_1
Content-Type: application/http
Content-Transfer-Encoding: binary
Content-ID: 1-2

POST UsageRecords/upsertByLogicalKey HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
 "value": {
 "category": "MEASURED",
 "metricId": "E_CHARGE",
 "technicalResourceId": "...",
 "startedAt": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z",
 "endedAt": "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z",
 "quantity": 1
 }
}

--changeset_1--

--batch_id-1778814615130-767-- Discard / Delete # Discard
v1: POST /usage-records/{id}/discard
v2: POST /UsageRecords({id})/discard

# Delete
v1: DELETE /usage-records/{id}
v2: DELETE /UsageRecords({id}) 

 4. Migrate Read Operations 
 List Usage Records v1 GET /usage-records
 ?filter=metricId eq 'API_CALL'
 and startedAt ge 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z
 &sort=startedAt desc
 &pageSize=50&pageNumber=1 v2 GET /UsageRecords
 ?$filter=metricId eq 'API_CALL'
 and startedAt ge 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z
 &$orderby=startedAt desc
 &$top=50 
 Pagination 
 The server automatically paginates results and returns @nextLink whenever more records exist. Always follow @nextLink to retrieve all pages. Case 1 — No $top specified (default page size: 16) GET /UsageRecords

# Response — up to 16 items, nextLink present if more exist
{
 "value": [ ...up to 16 items... ],
 "@nextLink": "UsageRecords?$skiptoken=..."
}

# Follow nextLink to get the next page
GET /UsageRecords?$skiptoken=... Case 2 — $top exceeds 100 (silently capped) 
 If $top is greater than 100, the server caps the result at 100 and returns @nextLink for the remainder — no error is returned. GET /UsageRecords?$top=500

# Response — only 100 items returned, rest via nextLink
{
 "value": [ ...100 items... ],
 "@nextLink": "UsageRecords?$top=500&$skiptoken=..."
} 
 Filter on Custom References v1 — Flat dot notation only ?filter=customReferences.typeCode eq 'SYSTEM_TYPE' v2 — Lambda operator ?$filter=customReferences/any(c:c/typeCode eq 'SYSTEM_TYPE') 

 5. Update Response Handling 
 v2 wraps collection responses in a standard OData envelope. Extract records from the value array; read count from @count i nstead of the x-count header. v1 — Plain array [{
 "id": "992e46d8-...",
 "isAssigned": true,
 "changedAt": "2026-09-15T12:00:00Z"
}] v2 — OData envelope {
 "@context": "$metadata#UsageRecords",
 "@count": 1,
 "value": [{
 "ID": "992e46d8-...",
 "assigned": true,
 "modifiedAt": "2026-09-15T12:00:00Z"
 }]
} 

 Migration Checklist 
 Change /v1 to /v2 in the base URL 
 Rename userTechnicalId → technicalResourceId , isAssigned → assigned , changedAt → modifiedAt , changedBy → modifiedBy , subscriptionNumber → subscriptionDocumentNumber 
 Change single-record write: POST /usage-records → POST /UsageRecords/upsertByLogicalKey with { "value": { ... } } 
 Change batch format: JSON → multipart/mixed 
 Change filter= → $filter= , sort= → $orderby= 
 Replace pageNumber / pageSize with @nextLink (recommended) or $top / $skip 
 Update count: x-count header → @count in response body 
 Update response parsing: root array → .value array 
 Update discard/delete URLs: /{id}/discard → ({id})/discard , /{id} → ({id}) 
 (Recommended) Add $select to reduce payload on read-heavy integrations 
 (Recommended) Replace multi-request patterns with $expand 
 Resources 
 API Guide — Usage Records 
 SAP Business Accelerator Hub — Usage Records v2 
 OData V4 Query Options Reference

title: SII Tip for Spain #15: SII and data consistency checks
author: FranciscoHurtado
text:
Introduction 
 Spain’s SII (Suministro Inmediato de Información) requires companies to submit invoice records to the AEAT tax authority within 4 days of posting (8 days for self-invoices). Beyond the submission deadline, Law 11/2021 of 9 July 2021 — on measures to prevent and combat tax fraud — introduced Article 29.2.j) of the General Tax Law , which obliges all accounting and invoicing systems to guarantee the integrity, preservation, accessibility, legibility, traceability, and unalterability of billing records, preventing interpolations, omissions, or alterations without a proper audit trail. 
 Meeting this obligation requires more than just sending the XML to the Tax Agency. You also need to verify that the records on both sides — your SAP system and the Tax Agency portal — remain consistent over time. There are three distinct layers of consistency to consider: 

 Layer 
 When it runs 
 Who checks 
 What it catches 

 Vaidations 
 At the moment of reception by the Tax Agency 
 Tax Agency (response codes) 
 Fiscal correctness of the data 

 SII application checks 
 During the SII eDocument creation or XML submission process 
 SAP ( ESSII_EDOCCREATE / ESSII_EDOCLIST ) 
 Configuration or data errors that prevent list submission 

 Consistency Checks 
 As a separate scheduled process 
 SAP Consistency Checks framework 
 Discrepancies between the records already in SAP and those already at the AEAT. 
 This blog focuses on the third layer — the Electronic Document Consistency Checks framework in SAP S/4HANA, Apps " Check Electronic Document Consistency " (F7494), " Resolve electronic Document Inconsistencies " (F7043), " Schedule Jobs for Electronic Document Consistency " (F7494) and " Display Electronic Document Consistency Logs" ( F8173 ). 
 Inconsistencies at this layer are silent by default: the system keeps running, invoices keep posting, and SII submissions keep going out — but some documents are in the wrong state, missing from one side, or have content differences you are unaware of. Left undetected, these discrepancies surface during period-end reviews or AEAT audits at the worst possible moment. 
 Any company with a Spanish company code subject to SII — typically with an annual turnover above 6 million Euros, or voluntarily opted in — runs monthly or even daily SII reporting cycles. The Consistency Checks framework is relevant for all of them, but it is especially critical in the following situations: 
 High-volume invoicing (retail, utilities, distribution) where communication timeouts between SAP and the AEAT are statistically inevitable. 
 Companies that use both SAP and a non-SAP billing platform, where some invoices may have been submitted to the AEAT directly and have no eDocument counterpart in SAP. 
 Companies that had to perform manual corrections directly on the AEAT portal (e.g., to deregister an invoice outside the normal SAP flow), leaving a content or status mismatch. 

 Inconsistency types 
 Not all inconsistencies look alike. The three layers introduced above each have a different failure signature: 
 Validation failures are returned by the AEAT as response codes when SAP submits a list. The Tax Agency's official Validations and Errors document defines three categories: structural (the entire request is rejected), syntactic (the invoice is rejected), and business (the invoice is registered but marked with errors that must be corrected). Common examples: 
 Error 3000 — Duplicate invoice. The Tax Agency already has a record for the same issuer NIF + invoice number + issue date combination. The most frequent error in practice. 
 Error 1157 — Incomplete VAT breakdown. The < DesgloseFactura> block must include at least one of < InversionSujetoPasivo> or < DesgloseIVA> . 
 Error 1166 — Invalid tax rate. The value in < TipoImpositivo> is not in the list of permitted values (common in Canary Islands IGIC scenarios). 
 Error 1579 — < CuotaDeducible> on a non-Spanish DUA must be 0 when < TipoFactura> is F5 . 
 Error 1279 — < CuotaDeducible> not allowed on simplified invoice type F2 . 
 SAP SII does not validate these business rules before submission and it is the customer’s responsibility to ensure data quality upstream. 
 SII Application failures surface during the SAP eDocument creation or list generation process ( ESSII_EDOCCREATE / ESSII_EDOCLIST ). A typical example is error EDOCUMENT_ES_SII 027 (“eDocument for source XXXX is not valid for lists”), which occurs when the Invoice ID is incomplete — a missing BP tax ID or invoice number field — and the eDocument ends up in NOT_VALID_FOR_BUND status. These errors are visible in the SII Cockpit (EDOC_COCKPIT) or in the " Manage Electronic Documents " App and are normally resolved by fixing the underlying source data. 
 Consistency Checks — the focus of this blog — are different. After a successful submission, the Tax Agency and SAP records can gradually drift apart. None of these generate an active error during day-to-day operations; they only surface when you actively run the Consistency Checks process: 
 eDocuments stuck in Registered with Errors or Missing Response in " Manage Electronic Documents" App or SII Cockpit even though the Tax Agency has long since accepted or deregistered the invoice. 
 An invoice that appears on the Tax Agency portal under your tax ID but has no corresponding eDocument in SAP — perhaps entered manually during a system outage. 
 An invoice SAP submitted successfully, but the Tax Agency portal shows Correcta while SAP still shows Rejected because the HTTP response was lost in transit. 
 A reversal journal entry posted in SAP, but the corresponding deregistration eDocument was never submitted to the Tax Agency. 
 A document whose field values (tax base, tax amount, reporting period) differ between the Tax Agency record and the SAP eDocument, caused by a manual edit on the Tax Agency portal after submission. 

 Consistency Checks and SII 
 SII is an asynchronous submission process. SAP sends an XML payload to the Tax Agency, and the Tax Agency responds asynchronously with an acceptance or rejection. This creates several known failure modes: 
 Lost response: SAP submits successfully and the Tax Agency registers the invoice, but the HTTP response never reaches SAP (network timeout, integration middleware restart). SAP records the eDocument as Missing Response or keeps it in Registered with Errors , while the Tax Agency side shows Correcta . 
 Wrong endpoint: The integration package SAP Document and Reporting Compliance: Electronic Tax Register Books for Spain was pointed at the Tax Agency test endpoint during testing and never updated. All submissions went to the sandbox; the production Tax Agency portal has no record of them. 
 Manual AEAT portal entry: An invoice was entered directly on the Tax Agency's portal — either during a system migration, a disaster recovery scenario, or because the customer wanted a correction that was not feasible in SAP at the time. The Tax Agency record exists; SAP has no matching eDocument. 
 Manual AEAT portal deregistration: An invoice was deregistered directly on the AEAT portal without going through SAP’s standard reversal flow ( EDOC_DEREGISTER ). SAP still shows the eDocument as Registered ; the Tax Agency shows it as Anulada . 
 Content editing on the AEAT portal: The Tax Agency or the company manually adjusted a field value on the portal (e.g., correcting a NIF or a tax amount). The eDocument in SAP was never updated, creating a content mismatch. 
 The Consistency Checks framework is designed specifically to detect all these scenarios systematically, not just on demand. 

 Consistency checks process end-to-end 
 The end-to-end process runs in five steps. The first step is a one-time setup; the remaining four are part of the regular operational cycle. 

 1. Configure the framework (one-time setup) 
 Before any check can run, you must activate the Consistency Checks framework for each company code. This is done through three Self-Service Configuration UI (SSCUI) activities in the Manage Your Solution app: 
 SSCUI 106403 — Enable Consistency Checks for Company Codes 

 This is the master switch. For each company code, you select: 
 Consistency Scenario — the business process to cover 
 Spain SII Supplier Invoice 
 Spain SII Customer Invoice 
 Comparison Type — which pair of documents to compare: eDocuments vs. the AEAT portal, or source documents (journal entries) vs. the eDocuments generated from them., such as: 
 Journal Entry vs. eDocument 
 SAP vs. Tax Authority 
 Reversal Journal Entry vs eDocument 
 Tax Authority vs. SAP 
 Electronic Document Types — the specific document types to include in the checks according to the comparison type , such as: 
 SII Incoming Invoice 
 SII Outgoing Invoice 
 ... 
 Check Types — which checks to activate per document type, such as: 
 If document data is consistent 
 If document data is consistent 
 If a journal entry exists 
 ... 
 SSCUI 106684 — Assign Journal Entry Types to Comparison Types 

 Required when you activate the source-document comparison type (journal entry vs. eDocument). For each consistency scenario and comparison type, you assign which journal entry types (formerly accounting document types) should be included in the scope of the comparison. 

 SSCUI 106707 — Define Tolerance Limits for Amount Mismatch 
 Configures acceptable amount differences for the Content Check. A Content Mismatch is only flagged if the difference exceeds the defined threshold. Two tolerance types are available: 
 Value — the absolute difference must exceed the fixed threshold (e.g., more than 0.01 EUR) to be flagged. 
 Percentage — the difference must exceed the configured percentage; the lesser of the percentage-derived limit and the fixed limit is applied. 

 2. Retrieve the latest invoice records from the Tax Agency 
 Before running the consistency checks, your SAP system needs an up-to-date copy of what the Tax Agency has on record. Use the Process eDocument Inbound Messages app (or transaction EDOC_INBOUND_MSG ) to pull the Tax Agency's invoice records into SAP. This is the data source that the comparison engine uses. 

 Normally this process should come together with "Schedule Job for document consistency", however, you may schedule this step individually: the Tax Agency data is the baseline for all comparisons. 

 3. Schedule the consistency check jobs 
 This app lets you configure and schedule automatic comparison runs for your company codes. 

 In the app, create a new job using the template “Automatic resolution of identified inconsistencies” . This template both detects and resolves inconsistencies that have a deterministic resolution (e.g., updating an eDocument process status to match the Tax Agency). For inconsistencies that require human interaction (e.g., content mismatches), it will detect and flag them but not auto-resolve. 
 Set the company codes and the SII scenarios ( ESSIIOUT for customer invoices, ESSIIOUT for supplier invoices) you want to cover. 
 Configure a recurring schedule — daily or weekly depending on your volume.

 This app shows all detected inconsistencies grouped by type. Use the filters to narrow down by company code, document type, or consistency result process.

title: Compensation publish to Employee Central when future-dated Compensation Information records already
author: Gunnar92
text:
Dear experts, 
 We regularly run into issues in SuccessFactors Compensation projects when employees already have future-dated Compensation Information records in Employee Central at the time of the publish, for example because of an agreed salary change or an upcoming FTE change (full-time to part-time). 
 Typical scenario: 
 The compensation cycle publishes a salary increase effective 1 January. 
 The employee already has a Compensation Information record effective 1 March due to an FTE change, with a pro-rated salary. 
 After the publish, the 1 March record still holds the old amount, so the increase is lost from that date on. 
 We are aware of the template setting “Enable forward propagation of Compensation Information changes when publishing from Compensation to Employee Central”. However, it only updates future records whose values are unchanged, so it does not help where the future record contains a different (for example pro-rated) amount. 
 Our questions: 
 Is there a leading practice for handling future-dated Compensation Information records in a compensation cycle? 
 How do you design the pay component model to minimise the issue? 
 Do you handle the remaining cases manually (report plus correction after publish), or have you automated this? 
 Any best practices, lessons learned or pointers to documentation would be much appreciated. 
 @xavierlegarrec 
 Thank you and best regards, 
 Gunnar
